questions.q: What specific action does Kisa Gotami take immediately after her son dies that shows she is in denial of his death?
questions.a: She carries her dead son's body from house to house asking for medicine to cure him. A wrong answer (e.g. "she cries" or "she buries him") reveals the student cannot distinguish between normal mourning and the specific irrational denial that drives the parable's plot — they miss that her ACTION (seeking medicine for a corpse) is the textual evidence of denial.

questions.q: Why do the villagers say "She has lost her senses" instead of offering sympathy or medicine? What does this reaction reveal about their understanding of death?
questions.a: The villagers recognize the finality of death — they know no medicine can revive the dead. Their blunt statement shows they accept mortality as irreversible, contrasting with Kisa Gotami's denial. A wrong answer (e.g. "they are cruel" or "they don't care") reveals the student misses the philosophical contrast: the villagers represent conventional acceptance of death, while Kisa Gotami represents the attachment that Buddha will challenge.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "textual evidence" — find ONE phrase from the story that shows Kisa Gotami's love for her son BEFORE his death, and explain how that love makes her grief more intense.
questions.a: "Her only son" (or "only child") — the word "only" quantifies her total emotional investment. A weak answer quotes generic sadness ("she wept") without linking to the CAUSE (exclusive love). This tests if students can connect character detail to emotional consequence — a core board exam skill.

questions.q: Analyse how the story's SETTING (moving from house to house) mirrors Kisa Gotami's INTERNAL state. Why doesn't she stay in one place?
questions.a: Her physical wandering mirrors her mental inability to accept a fixed reality (death). She moves because staying still would force acceptance. A wrong answer describes the setting literally ("she walks through the village") without the metaphorical link — showing inability to analyse setting as psychological reflection, a key literary analysis skill.

questions.q: Evaluate: Is Kisa Gotami's behaviour "madness" or "love pushed to its limit"? Defend your view using the text.
questions.a: It is love pushed to its limit — the text never calls her mad; the villagers say "lost her senses" but Buddha later treats her with compassion, not correction. A wrong answer takes the villagers' view uncritically ("she is mad") showing inability to evaluate perspective and authorial stance — a competency question trap.

questions.q: Create a 3-line diary entry Kisa Gotami might write THAT NIGHT before meeting Buddha, using first-person voice and showing her mental state without using the word "sad".
questions.a: Example: "I knocked on every door. No one had the medicine. My arms ache from carrying him, but I cannot put him down — if I do, he is truly gone." Criteria: shows denial, physical detail, emotional truth. A poor entry writes "I am very sad" — telling not showing, lacking textual fidelity.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Kisa Gotami's grief refers to the intense, all-consuming sorrow of a young mother who loses her only child, leading her to carry the dead body from house to house begging for medicine to revive him — this initial stage of the parable ______ the raw, irrational nature of unprocessed grief before spiritual awakening begins.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you lose your phone with all your photos, contacts, and memories — you'd frantically ______ every room, retrace every step, maybe even ask strangers if they've seen it.
What is Kisa Gotami's grief? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Kisa Gotami's grief refers to the intense, all-consuming sorrow of a young mother who loses her only child, leading her to carry the dead body from house to house begging for medicine to revive him — this initial stage of the parable illustrates the raw, irrational nature of unprocessed grief before spiritual awakening begins.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Kisa Gotami's grief?
questions.a: Students think Kisa Gotami is "foolish" or "superstitious" for seeking medicine for a dead child — they miss that her action stems from LOVE so deep it temporarily overrides reason.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to (1) trace Kisa Gotami's emotional journey from denial to desperate action using specific textual evidence, and (2) explain how her grief represents the universal human condition of attachment that Buddha's teaching addresses.
